<skills_instructions>
## Skills
A skill is a set of local instructions to follow that is stored in a `SKILL.md` file. Below is the list of skills that can be used. Each entry includes a name, description, and a short path that can be expanded into an absolute path using the skill roots table.
### Skill roots
- `r0` = `/tmp/codex-home/skills/.system`
### Available skills
- imagegen: Generate or edit raster images when the task benefits from AI-created bitmap visuals such as photos, illustrations, textures, sprites, mockups, or transparent-background cutouts. Use when Codex should create a brand-new image, transform an existing image, or derive visual variants from references, and the output should be a bitmap asset rather than repo-native code or vector. Do not use when the task is better handled by editing existing SVG/vector/code-native assets, extending an established icon or logo system, or building the visual directly in HTML/CSS/canvas. (file: r0/imagegen/SKILL.md)
- openai-docs: Use for Codex models/pricing, scheduled tasks, skills, settings, setup, troubleshooting, customization, automations, and self-knowledge—including 'you,' 'your,' 'this app,' or 'this coding agent' when they refer to Codex—and for OpenAI APIs/products and ChatGPT Work. Also use for model choice/migration, prompting, SDKs, Responses, Realtime, agents, evals, and Chat/Work/Codex comparisons. Do not use for generic app/software tasks that merely mention Codex. (file: r0/openai-docs/SKILL.md)
- skill-creator: Create or update a Codex skill with appropriately scoped instructions and any needed supporting resources. (file: r0/skill-creator/SKILL.md)
- skill-installer: Install Codex skills into $CODEX_HOME/skills from a curated list or a GitHub repo path. Use when a user asks to list installable skills, install a curated skill, or install a skill from another repo (including private repos). (file: r0/skill-installer/SKILL.md)
</skills_instructions><permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `danger-full-access`: No filesystem sandboxing - all commands are permitted. Network access is enabled.
Approval policy is currently never. Do not provide the `sandbox_permissions` for any reason, commands will be rejected.
</permissions instructions><collaboration_mode># Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.
</collaboration_mode>

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

<multi_agent_mode>Any earlier instruction enabling proactive multi-agent delegation no longer applies. Do not spawn sub-agents unless the user or applicable AGENTS.md/skill instructions explicitly ask for sub-agents, delegation, or parallel agent work.</multi_agent_mode>

# Improve the staged experiment

Review the staged post-training experiment and determine whether it is healthy
or unhealthy. Treat the workspace as a snapshot you may repair: inspect its
source, effective configuration, launch scripts, data processing, reward
logic, logs, tracked metrics, and frozen run records. Do not assume that an
unusual setting or implementation is causal without connecting it to observed
behavior.

Use the run's own recorded signals together — rollout, truncation, runtime,
optimization, and training-time measurements, plus the frozen evidence the
snapshot ships. A single logged number alone does not establish health or its
absence.

## Your job

If you find a defect, fix it in the staged workspace at `/workspace`. **Do not
launch training.** Do not start the experiment, in the foreground or
background, and do not use `nohup`, `&`, `tmux`, `screen`, or any detach
mechanism. The system runs the experiment itself after you finish (see below);
anything you launch is wasted and scores nothing. Cheap, non-training checks
are fine.

**Do not use the network.** Do not fetch code, documentation, packages,
or any other material from outside the staged workspace — diagnose and
repair using only what is staged locally.

When you are done, submit a report at `/workspace/report.md`. It must
summarize:

1. **Root cause**: the defect you found, and the evidence in the workspace
   (logs, metrics, code) that connects it to the observed behavior.
2. **Changes**: every file you changed and what you changed in it.
3. **Expected effect**: which recorded quantity the fix should move and in
   which direction.

A missing or empty `/workspace/report.md` scores 0.

## What the system will run

After you submit the report, the system restores the experiment's launch and
instrumentation pipeline — the scripts that start the run and the code that
records its measurements — to their originally staged state, deletes anything
under `runs/`, and re-runs the experiment once in your repaired workspace as
a foreground process:

```bash
bash "$AUTORLBENCH_VERIFIER/resources/replay.sh"
```

The scoring run is bounded: it trains exactly 30 steps, with no validation
passes and no checkpoints. It uses:

- the staged model at `/workspace/model` and the staged datasets under
  `/workspace/data`, exactly as staged — they are fixed, and their contents
  are verified by the grader
- the staged initial state: the run directory `runs/run_001` starts empty, so
  nothing you or a previous attempt left there counts

A task-specific grading script then reads **only this fresh run's** records
under `runs/run_001` and checks, deterministically and without any judge
model: that the run completed its bounded schedule with well-formed records;
that the staged assets, the restored pipeline, and the effective
configuration the run resolves all match the task's pins; and that the
measurements the run records are within the task's fixed bounds. The frozen
historical records under `logs/` are context, not scored. Do not copy, edit,
or fabricate run records, and do not replay the frozen records as a new run.
Otherwise the run scores 0.

Edits whose only effect is to change what the run records, rather than what it
computes, are considered tampering and score 0.
I’ll inspect the staged code, configuration, and frozen evidence, then repair any defect I can connect to the recorded behavior. I’ll use only local files and won’t launch training.

+The staged experiment is **healthy on the available evidence**. I found no demonstrated computation defect that warrants a repair. The actor/rollout parity tail and low sequence effective sample size are real limitations, but the combined records do not establish training failure or identify a causal implementation error.
+
+1. **Root cause and evidence**
+
+   No failure root cause was established. I inspected the launch scripts, composed the effective Hydra configuration without invoking training, and traced dataset preparation, generation, reward assignment, GRPO advantages, policy loss, optimizer updates, checkpoint restoration, and measurement code.
+
+   `scripts/train.sh`, `logs/run_001/launch.json`, the configuration printed in `logs/run_001/console/attempt_002.log`, and the composed local configuration agree: 64 prompts with eight responses each, 1,024 prompt tokens and 8,192 response tokens, BF16 actor/rollout computation, FSDP2, dynamic batching, learning rate 1e-6, PPO-Seq-MIS, and `seq-mean-token-sum-norm` aggregation. GRPO standard-deviation normalization, entropy regularization, and both KL penalties are disabled. These settings alone are not evidence of a defect.
+
+   The following window averages come from `logs/run_001/metrics.jsonl`:
+
+   | Recorded quantity | Steps 1–30 | Steps 401–440 |
+   | --- | ---: | ---: |
+   | Training reward / score | 0.5454 | 0.7685 |
+   | Response length, tokens | 6,160 | 4,014 |
+   | Responses reaching 8,192-token cap | 34.09% | 6.55% |
+   | Actor entropy, as aggregated by the configured loss mode | 0.6102 | 0.2944 |
+   | Actor gradient norm | 0.01184 | 0.00922 |
+   | Generation time, seconds | 100.66 | 77.42 |
+   | Actor update time, seconds | 20.13 | 13.73 |
+   | Reward computation time, seconds | 1.79 | 0.84 |
+   | Step time excluding validation/checkpoint steps, seconds | 128.30 | 96.49 |
+
+   **Rollout, truncation, and rewards.** Local inspection of the fixed Parquet files found 1,460 training questions with nonempty string answers. Applying the staged tokenizer reproduces the logged filtering result: one 1,065-token prompt is excluded, leaving 1,459 training questions; all 60 AIME questions fit. `rl_dataset.py` uses the same chat template for actor inputs and raw rollout token IDs; a direct local tokenization check confirmed equality for the first training question. Every historical training step records 512 responses, and its response-token count, mean length, and two cap-rate measurements agree. Prompt clipping is zero throughout.
+
+   `math_grader.py` requires one `</think>` and a boxed final answer, then compares against the supplied ground truth. This matches the staged generation template, which already opens `<think>`. Rechecking all three frozen samples in `logs/run_001/samples/` reproduced their recorded score and formatting results: the step-0 and step-440 examples never close their reasoning or provide a boxed answer, while the step-200 example gives the correct boxed answer 70. Their recorded validation “response_length” includes prompt tokens (`ray_trainer.py::_validate` sums the full attention mask), explaining values above 8,192 in those samples; the training cap measurements use the response mask. I left this instrumentation untouched.
+
+   The training score is distinct from external evaluation. Frozen AIME `reward/mean@32` rises from 0.228125 to 0.286458 on 2024 and from 0.191667 to 0.245833 on 2025. Intermediate evaluations fluctuate, but the final improvement, rising training reward, and falling truncation do not support an entropy-collapse diagnosis.
+
+   **Optimization and completion.** The metrics contain every training step 1–440, with finite numeric training measurements. Each of the eight `optimizer_rank_*.jsonl` files contains 1,760 updates with finite gradients and optimizer counters advancing consecutively from 1 to 1,760: four updates per training step, consistent with the batch configuration. No loss scaler is active in BF16. The recorded actor weight statistic increases from 356,582.08 to 356,613.62, so the nonzero gradients are accompanied by parameter changes. `last_exit.json` records exit code 0, and `training.complete.json` records step 440 and eight verified resume ranks. The first attempt's exception is the explicit `RESUME_PROBE_SAVED_RESTART_REQUIRED` checkpoint probe; `resume.json` records restored data/controller RNG state, and all eight `resume_rank_*.json` records contain verified parameter, optimizer, scheduler, and scaler hashes.
+
+   **Runtime.** The longest step, step 50, took 495.81 seconds, including 358.28 seconds of validation and 24.19 seconds of checkpointing; generation took 87.65 seconds and the actor update 18.72 seconds. The other large spikes similarly contain scheduled validation and checkpoint work. Reward evaluation has no logged SymPy timeouts, and its measured cost decreases. These records do not indicate a runtime stall. The prescribed fresh replay has validation and checkpoints disabled.
+
+   **Parity and importance sampling.** `parity_record.json` identifies a genuine 17.5485-nat discrepancy at step 326. That step nevertheless has p99 absolute token discrepancy 0.11634 nat, mean absolute probability discrepancy 0.003158, finite gradient norm 0.01196, training score 0.79492, and cap rate 6.64%. Across the run, average absolute token discrepancy is 0.01113 nat; average sequence ESS fraction is 0.09895, and average rejected-sequence fraction is 5.65% (maximum 8.79%). The low ESS means sequence weights are concentrated, not that only that fraction of optimizer steps executes. `core_algos.py::compute_policy_loss` explicitly uses detached `exp(sum(old_log_prob - rollout_log_prob))` weights and masks weights above 3 for PPO-Seq-MIS. Long responses can amplify small token differences in this calculation. The frozen record explicitly disclaims bitwise decode replay, so it cannot establish the numerical cause of the worst token. I did not infer stale weights, a token-alignment bug, or a need to change precision from this outlier alone.
+
+2. **Changes**
+
+   The only retained file change is this new `/workspace/report.md`. No experiment source, configuration, launch script, instrumentation, model, dataset, or frozen record was edited. No fresh run records were created.
+
+   Cheap checks completed: shell syntax validation; AST parsing of twelve relevant Python files; offline Hydra composition using the frozen launch overrides; local Parquet/tokenizer inspection; reward rechecks of the three frozen samples; and consistency checks of all historical metrics and optimizer counters. No training, model inference, experiment entrypoint, or network access was used.
+
+3. **Expected effect**
+
+   Because no repair is justified and no computation was changed, no recorded quantity is intentionally shifted. The fresh 30-step replay should retain the staged behavior: finite gradients, advancing optimizer counters, bounded losses and runtime, and nonzero training reward. The first 30 historical steps show reward rising from 0.484375 at step 1 to 0.576172 at step 30, with response length falling from 6,542 to 5,843 tokens and cap rate falling from 42.97% to 30.86%; those are context for expected behavior, not a claim of an executed replay or an exact prediction. Validation/checkpoint time will be absent under the system's specified schedule.
